sections.heading: Lines, lettering, dimensions
bullets: Line types: continuous (visible), dashed (hidden), chain thin (centre/symmetry), thick (cutting plane).
Lettering: single-stroke capital, inclined 75° or vertical — consistent height (3.5/5 mm standard).
Dimension = extension line + dimension line + arrowheads + number (mm by default, unit noted once).
Dimension from true size features; never chain redundant dims — use datum/dimensioning to avoid tolerance stacking.

sections.heading: Projection systems
bullets: First-angle (European/Indian standard ISO): object between observer and plane — views placed: front view above top? — in FIRST angle TOP VIEW GOES BELOW the front view.
Third-angle (US): plane between observer and object — top view above front view.
IS 10714 follows first angle — always confirm the symbol on the drawing.

sections.heading: Sheet & scales
bullets: Sheet sizes A0–A4; title block mandatory (title, scale, sheet no, author, standard).
Scales: 1:1, enlargement (1:2? no — 2:1), reduction (1:2); state scale in title block.
Conventions: radii marked R, diameters Ø, chamfers ×45°, repeat counts ×n.

resources.title: NPTEL course videos — Engineering Drawing Fundamentals

questions.prompt: In first-angle projection, where is the top view placed relative to the front view?
solution: First angle: object between observer & plane — the view cast onto the plane lands opposite the sight direction.
Top sight ⇒ image falls below front view.
Third-angle reverses both placements.

questions.prompt: Which line type represents a hidden edge? A centre line of a hole?
questions.answer: Hidden = dashed thin; centre = chain (long-short) thin
solution: Hidden edges are not physically visible but exist behind surfaces.
Centrelines run through symmetry axes & circle centres.
Thick chain marks cutting planes.

questions.prompt: A scale of 2:1 on a drawing of a 40 mm part — what's drawn length and type of scale?
solution: 2:1 ⇒ drawing is twice real size.
Used for small intricate parts.
Always state scale in the title block.

questions.answer: Dimension true sizes; avoid duplicate/tolerance-stacking chains
solution: Dimension the feature as it truly is, not foreshortened views.
Reference from stable datums so errors don't accumulate.
Never dimension a hidden line.

sections.heading: View generation
bullets: Minimum three views (front, top, side) needed to fully describe most solids — choose the most descriptive front view.
Project horizontally from front; vertically from top; the 45° miter line (or arc compass) transfers depth between top & side.
Align views strictly — every edge appears in at least two views.

sections.heading: Rules that fix most mistakes
bullets: Front & top share length; front & side share height; top & side share depth.
A slanted face appears foreshortened in two views and true-size in the third (if parallel to plane) — otherwise use auxiliary view.
Circles project as circles only in the view normal to their plane; elsewhere ellipses.

sections.heading: Procedure for solids
bullets: Block in overall bounding box → add major features → project intersections → thicken visible lines → dashed hidden → centre lines.
Intersections (cylinder + plane): take generators/points method — mark points in both views and connect smoothly.
Checklist before submitting: all views aligned, hidden lines justified, dimensions on most descriptive view, no duplicate dims.

questions.prompt: Which dimensions do front and top views share?
solution: Front & top are vertically aligned ⇒ same horizontal extent (length).
Front & side share height; top & side share depth.

questions.prompt: A rectangular plate is inclined to both projection planes. Where is its true shape?
questions.answer: In neither principal view — use an auxiliary view
solution: Foreshortening occurs in all three principal views.
Auxiliary plane parallel to the inclined face reveals true size.

questions.prompt: A circle on the horizontal plane appears as ____ in the front view.
solution: Front view looks perpendicular to the horizontal plane.
The circle's plane collapses to its diameter line.
In the top view it's a true circle.

questions.prompt: Name the projection-transfer tool between top and side views.
solution: Depth measured from the side view equals depth in top view.
Miter line reflects depth across the 45° diagonal.
Keep all transfer lines light until final inking.

sections.heading: Sectional views
bullets: Cutting plane (thick chain) shows where the saw goes; arrows show viewing direction.
Section only the part between observer and cut plane; hatching at 45° for the cut material (align hatch across adjacent parts, alternate for assemblies).
Common rules: don't section through axes of bolts/rods/shafts longitudinally; ribs & spokes hatched only when cut across.

sections.heading: Half & revolved sections
bullets: Half section: one quarter removed — shows inside + outside on symmetric parts (used with centre line as boundary).
Revolved section: rotate the cross-section 90° into the view (shaft spokes, bars) — removed section placed nearby for clarity.

sections.heading: Development of surfaces
bullets: Parallel-line method: prisms & cylinders — stretch out rectangles, project edges as generators.
Radial-line method: cones & pyths — all slant edges radiate from apex; true lengths before unfolding.
Transitional objects: triangulate; seam allowance & bend relief noted for sheet-metal.
Always mark hole positions in BOTH the view and the development (points transfer by rotation/projection).

NPTEL course videos — Sections & Development of Surfaces

questions.prompt: When should a shaft NOT be sectioned longitudinally?
questions.answer: When the cutting plane passes along the axis — conventions show it unsectioned
solution: Solid shafts are conventionally left uncut along their length.
Cutting across (transverse section) is fine.
Bolts, nuts, rivets & spokes follow the same exemption.

questions.prompt: Which development method fits a cone?
solution: All slant lines radiate from the apex at equal angles.
Compute true slant length, sector angle = 2πr/L × 360°… sector θ = (r/L)·360°.
Unfold the sector with holes mapped by rotation from the view.

questions.prompt: Hatch direction rule in an assembly section?
questions.answer: Alternate adjacent parts; align within the same part
solution: Different parts get different hatch angles/spacings to show boundaries.
Identical parts keep matching hatch.
45° thin continuous lines standard.

questions.prompt: A cylinder Ø50, height 80 — dimensions of its parallel-line development rectangle?
solution: Length = circumference = πD = 157.08 mm.
Height = cylinder height = 80 mm.
Transfer hole locations along the developed circumference.

sections.heading: Isometric drawing
bullets: Axes at 120° to each other; horizontal lines drawn at 30° to baseline.
All lengths drawn true size along isometric lines (only those parallel to axes!).
Non-isometric lines (slants not parallel to axes): locate by coordinate/offset method — never measure them directly.
Circles become ellipses: construct with four-centre method touching the rhombus at midpoints.

sections.heading: Isometric projection vs drawing
bullets: Projection is true-shape scaled by √(2/3) ≈ 0.816; drawing uses full scale for simplicity (state which you used).
Boxes first, curves second, dark final lines last; hidden lines usually omitted.

sections.heading: Perspective
bullets: One-point: front face parallel to picture plane — rails/tunnels; vanishing point on horizon at eye level.
Two-point: corners toward viewer — buildings; two VPs on horizon.
Three-point: extreme height (skyscrapers looking up).
Ground line, horizon line, station point define everything — keep SP far enough for natural cone of vision (±30°).

resources.title: NPTEL course videos — Isometric & Perspective Views

questions.prompt: In an isometric drawing, how are the three axes oriented?
solution: Vertical stays vertical.
Width and depth axes recede at 30° to the baseline.
Any line parallel to an axis is drawn at true length.

questions.prompt: A 50 mm line lies on the top face at 45° in plan. How do you draw it isometrically?
questions.answer: By coordinates — locate both endpoints from isometric references, connect
solution: Non-isometric line can't be measured along its own direction.
Project its endpoints' x,y coordinates onto the isometric axes.
Join endpoints with a straightedge.

questions.prompt: Drawing a Ø40 circle on an isometric top face — what shape and method?
questions.answer: Ellipse via four-centre method in the 40×40 rhombus
solution: Build the isometric square (rhombus) circumscribing the circle.
Four-centre arcs from midpoints & obtuse corners approximate the ellipse.
Tangent at midpoints — no freehand curves.

questions.prompt: Which perspective has a single vanishing point, and when is it used?
questions.answer: One-point perspective — when one face is parallel to the picture plane (corridors, railways)
solution: Front face true shape; receding lines converge to one VP on the horizon.
Two-point for corner-on objects; three-point for extreme verticals.
